item.description: The cyberattack on Alternative for Germany (AfD), the country’s most prominent far-right political party, exposed hundreds of thousands of confidential emails and attachments, as well as more than 345,000 unique email addresses. Have I Been Pwned confirmed the scale of the breach for the first time today, after AfD officially disclosed the September attack on its hosting provider last week. AfD said in its statement that “only a few email accounts were illegally copied,” but admitted a large amount of the data was taken from them, resulting in an extensive data breach. The emails were added to what the party described as “an activist website,” which summarised the email chains into searchable topics and has led to the publication of various revelations, such as a party co-leader’s opinions on colleagues’ “deeply problematic” racial discourse . Per a report from investigative journalist Lilith Wittmann, citing conversations with the cybercriminals responsible for the hack-and-leak job and party sources, the attack was first spotted on September 9 and started with a compromise of a poorly protected WordPress site. The same report claimed the criminals gained persistent access to the servers operated by the hosting provider, identified as AfD-owned Alternita Dienstleistungs GmbH, and exfiltrated more than a terabyte of data. Furthermore, it is an attack on the German party system and thus on democracy. “We are extremely worried that, apparently, the content of the stolen documents was analyzed using a very rudimentary AI. This analysis focused on keywords, not the context. The alleged scandals published so far do not stand up to scrutiny – a fact that, thankfully, is being confirmed by a growing number of commentators on social media.” Among the AI-generated summaries compiled by the “activist site” are chains supposedly expressing views related to Holocaust denial, racist and antisemitic rants, the 9/11 disaster, forged documents, and more. item.description: The British government has been busy courting AI datacenter companies while apparently finding little time to speak to the people who will have to live next door to their enormous server farms. That’s according to a report published Tuesday by campaign group Spotlight on Corruption, which found that 84 percent of the stakeholders ministers met with to discuss datacenters between July 2024 and June 2026 were businesses or private-sector trade associations. Environmental groups, by contrast, didn't get a single meeting with ministers or senior officials. The findings raise questions about who gets a say in Britain's AI Growth Zones, which the government hopes will attract billions of pounds in investment by making it easier and cheaper to build the infrastructure needed to power its AI ambitions. According to the report, titled Zoned Out, ministers met representatives from 137 different businesses during the two-year period, while permanent secretaries and directors general held no meetings with community groups about datacenters. Local residents didn't fare much better. Ministers met just two community groups, both after decisions had already been made to designate their areas as AI Growth Zones. In one case, the meeting took place on the very day the designation was announced. The government also failed to conduct a national public consultation on its AI Growth Zone strategy, despite the potential consequences for electricity supplies , water consumption , and local communities . Spotlight found no independent consultations with residents in the selected areas, although some developers conducted their own. Even local councils appear to have struggled to get a hearing. Of the ten local authorities and devolved governments affected by the five announced zones, half reported no communication with ministers or senior DSIT officials beyond their applications. Two had exchanged brief emails, while another secured a 15-minute meeting with a junior minister. The government has been more accommodating to the companies building these facilities. AI Growth Zones offer developers faster planning decisions and better access to electricity infrastructure, with the aim of rapidly expanding Britain's computing capacity. As we reported in March , the government has also been consulting on proposals that could allow strategically important datacenters to jump the electricity grid connection queue, potentially ahead of housing developments already waiting for power. item.description: Omarchy has already taken up plenty of our column inches, but a new tentacle is reaching into the hitherto untouched FreeBSD. Daemonarchy brings Omarchy's Wayland-based desktop to the BSD world. It's an independent effort by Jordan Hubbard, one of the original founders of the FreeBSD project, and it's unaffiliated with the original Linux-based Omarchy. We looked at Omarchy in August and didn’t like it much. It isn't exactly a Linux distribution. That implies it's a coherent set of packages managed as a whole by uniform tools. Omarchy is a collection of apps and preconfigured settings, packaged up with the help of LLM bots and put up for download. You have to update it using its own special script, rather than the standard tools of the underlying Arch Linux – and in our testing, that update script fell over with error messages when running in a VM. However, there's no such thing as a bad press, and Omarchy is popular and growing. It keeps on attracting sponsorship as well as new users migrating from Windows and macOS, who seem to relish its bizarre, inconsistent, and ad hoc UI as a challenge: trying to close a window in Hyprland, the tiling compositor that forms the core of Omarchy's UI. In Omarchy, windows don't have title bars, let alone anything as old-fashioned as window control buttons you can click. To close a window, you must use a keystroke. In most Linux windowing environments, that's the standard Alt-F4 . Not here. Next, we tried Super+W – on a Mac, that's Command+W , which has meant "close the window" since 1984 or so. Still no. We found an answer on Reddit – it's Super + C. Daemonarchy is not directly related. It's a collection of FreeBSD ports of the various tools and components that went into Omarchy, individually adapted to run on FreeBSD, and collected together into an installable ISO image. The current release is version 1.3.1 . Remarkably, in approximately 10 days, Daemonarchy has gone through 10 releases . Multiple packages are recent ports by jkh@freebsd.org – the email address of Jordan Hubbard. If the name rings a bell, he was one of the original founders of the FreeBSD project, and has had an interesting career in which he’s worked at various companies. The Register first mentioned him by name 25 years ago, when Wind River bought BSD/OS vendors BSDi . By the following year, Hubbard was at Apple , where he helped freshen up the BSD-based Unix layer underneath the new Mac OS X. In 2015, he helped launch the NextBSD project to modernize FreeBSD with Apple Darwin components, which as we reported in July was recently restarted. The new NextBSD effort is being built with the help of LLM coding assistants. item.title: Year of Linux on the Beach confirmed
item.description: 2026 might not be the Year of Linux on the Desktop, but it is certainly the Year of Linux on the Beachfront, judging by some digital signage at the Spanish resort of Lloret de Mar. Snapped by Rich Skuse, an aficionado of automotive shonk, this sign skips the town's attractions or useful information entirely. Instead, it gives away its Ubuntu and Firefox roots with an update prompt and a perky "Welcome back," suggesting someone has turned it off and on again. As this signage is likely connected to the Internet, that Ubuntu update is probably a good idea. 26.04.1 is the latest LTS version and contains a raft of tweaks and improvements. Sadly, we expect beachgoers are probably more interested in sun, sand, and sangria than in keeping a Linux installation in tip-top shape. The sign is a recent addition to the Passeig d'Agustí Font. Behind the photographer stand palm trees, with a beach and the azure waters of the Mediterranean Sea beyond. Lloret de Mar underwent several renovations ahead of the 2026 summer season, and we guess the sign was one of them, since it wasn't there in April 2025 (according to a well-known ad slinger). According to Lloret Gaceta, a publication for the region, "The goal is to continue evolving into a more modern, sustainable, accessible, and higher-quality tourist destination, adapted to the new demands of residents and visitors." Readers might be interested to learn that part of this evolution includes a ban on selling alcoholic beverages in containers larger than one liter at beach bars. A few too many adult drinks could explain the configuration that led to this bork, or perhaps an engineer took one look outside, at another balmy day, and decided "that'll do" when it came to configuring the signage. Either way, this is a tourist destination, and the last thing the average administrator wants to be reminded of on their vacation is the need to keep code up to date. As such, we suspect many will simply ignore the distressed digital display and instead seek out somewhere shady to sit, where the seafront can be admired, beverages consumed, and the bork…? Well, it's somebody else's problem. ®

item.title: How everyday technology choices drive true workplace sustainability
item.description: For many members of the C-suite these days, sustainability is a top three agenda item alongside technology and AI adoption, according to research from Deloitte. In fact, the report says, technology is considered a vital means of hitting organizational goals here, with the implementation of IT solutions being the most common approach for doing so. The importance of tech's role in this context is reflected in the views of IT decision-makers themselves. A recent survey, conducted by Barco ClickShare , revealed that 96 percent of the 500 US tech leaders questioned consider their sustainability activities to make a significant and positive global contribution to strategy here. A further 98 percent feel their departments should lead the way in such activities. Indeed, more than four out of five felt so strongly about the situation that they would turn down a job offer at a new employer if it did not have a strong sustainability track record, they said. Yannic Laleeuwe is Marketing Director Workplace Collaboration at wireless conferencing and collaboration platform provider, Barco ClickShare. She believes IT functions have this central role to play in tackling sustainability issues because many of their "day-to-day technology choices directly influence an organization's environmental footprint". "Sustainability is about practical decisions: buying reliable technology, extending product life, reducing complexity, and ensuring devices can be managed, repaired and responsibly recycled," Laleeuwe explains. Sustainability as a collaborative practice But given that technology-related decisions are rarely made by IT leaders alone, it is clear they cannot tackle sustainability challenges alone either. As Barco ClickShare's report indicates, a mere 6 percent of IT departments are the sole decision-makers on tech investments, which includes meeting room systems. This means that collaboration with other stakeholders is vital. Such stakeholders include not only sustainability and environmental affairs teams. They also consist of procurement, finance, facilities management, operations, and executive leaders. "Working together, it's possible to balance security, usability, cost, lifecycle impact, energy efficiency, repairability and end-of-life recovery before a purchase is even made," Laleeuwe points out. In other words, by collaborating, it becomes much easier to embed sustainability considerations into day-to-day activities. This includes maintaining and upgrading equipment properly to extend its life. It is these everyday IT decisions that can make all the difference in shaping behavior in the digital workplace. One example of this relates to the procurement process itself, which is often complex. item.title: Elvis rightsholders sue Anthropic for stealing songs and leaving them in Heartbreak Hotel
item.description: A supergroup of rights holders who own or control Elvis Presley songs have sued Anthropic for copyright infringement, alleging that the AI company stole The King’s works to train its AI models. “The Elvis Plaintiffs bring this action to enforce these exclusive rights against the Defendant that has built its entire business model based on copyright infringement at a scale never seen before,” states a complaint [PDF] filed last Friday in the United States District Court for the Northern District of California. Despite owning 274 Elvis songs, the titles of which offer many apt metaphors to illustrate the plaintiffs’ grievances, the lawsuit uses a Shakesperean allusion. “Defendant Anthropic has essentially put to the test the adage of whether monkeys and typewriters could, provided enough time, recreate Hamlet,” the complaint states. “However, rather than wait out the ‘infinite’ amount of time the infinite monkey theorem posits is necessary for said monkeys with typewriters to randomly, one letter at a time, string together that famous question of ‘To be or not to be?’, Anthropic found a workaround.” “Rather than training its monkeys from first principles, Anthropic found mimicry (i.e. copyright infringement) to be the much easier pursuit.” The lawsuit uses riffs that will sound familiar to anyone who has followed the many allegations that AI companies hoovered up any content they could find to train their models: Fair use doctrines don’t apply to all content used to train AI models; Anthropic should have known that some of the torrents and datasets it used for model training were either licensed (and therefore not freely usable), or stolen; The AI company should know it needs a license before allowing its Claude products to do things like produce the lyrics to Elvis songs when prompted to do so; Chatbots cost rights-holders money when users prompt them to produce create content “in the style of” artists whose works are subject to copyright. The plaintiffs want damages and a slice of Anthropic’s profits, or $150,000 per work. The latter values damages at $41.1 million. Anthropic has reportedly vowed to defend the matter, but has already resolved a similar case in which it was accused of training its models on books without seeking or securing permission from the authors. The AI upstart created a $1.5 billion fund to compensate writers to make that one go away. The plaintiffs note that Anthropic has billions of cash on hand and plans a mega-float (which it announced today ) so can afford to indulge in A Little Less Conversation, Don’t Be Cruel, stop being The Devil In Disguise, and Patch It Up by paying up. ®

GMO runs a service called Onamae.com Desktop Cloud and last week admitted “a third party had installed malicious programs in the server environments of some customers.” That’s never welcome news but is an especially poor outcome because the servers host cloudy Windows desktops that GMO recommends customers use to host foreign exchange trading applications. The next day, the company advised users to immediately change passwords for their trading accounts, and to do so using a device that they don’t use for trading. item.description: OpenAI has added a mid-range model to its GPT-6.1 family, offering strong performance at a lower price. The AI business' general-purpose models span four tiers. Products named "Sol" or "Astra" are its high-end offerings and come with price tags to match. "Luna" models are its cheapest offerings. This new model gets the "Terra" treatment the company reserves for mid-range models. "Terra continues to advance the cost-intelligence frontier across our model families, providing a new balance of speed, capability, and cost," OpenAI said . "Its standard API prices are 50 percent lower than those of GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-6.1 Sol, making it practical for developers to automate high-volume work, like reading incoming invoices and entering their details into accounting software." Artificial Analysis, a site that tracks model performance and cost, notes that GPT-6.1 Terra pushes the cost efficiency frontier. "It is the first Terra-class model since GPT-5.6, and is more intelligent for less than a third of the cost," the site says. In a comment posted to Hacker News, Ted Sanders, a member of technical staff at OpenAI, framed the differences between the various GPT-6.1 models thus: "In the case of GPT-6.1 Terra, I'd say Terra is probably better than Astra and Sol at technical communication, similar on vision and computer use (but much faster!), and a bit worse on most other things. item.title: Worm armed 42 GitHub repos by hiding a payload too big to fail
item.description: A new Miasma-family npm worm , originally believed to be just a test with no victims, secretly armed 42 real GitHub repositories from 11 owners, hijacking accounts as early as July and using a stealthy payload built to stay hidden from GitHub and automated scanners, according to JFrog researchers. Threat hunters at SafeDep, an open source supply chain security firm, first spotted the “testmetest” npm campaign last week, identifying 18 packages linked to the same operator between October 19 and October 25, including releases containing credential-stealing malware. As with earlier npm worms, the malware is self-replicating, steals credentials, and installs a wiper that deletes the home directory when the victim revokes the stolen GitHub token, the security researchers noted. The new npm worm shares code with June’s Miasma Phantom Gyp worm, and adds Mini Shai-Hulud’s token-revocation wiper. As of October 22, however, SafeDep had found no compromised third-party packages or victims. “All observed activity belongs to the operator’s own test accounts,” the team wrote. As with most happy-ending security stories, that proved too good to be true. In a Monday report, supply chain security company JFrog said its analysis proved otherwise , and found the testmetest campaign operator “had already armed real repositories belonging to established developers and organizations.” This isn’t just about timing, either, according to JFrog researchers Guy Korolevski and Yair Benamou. “The payload blobs were large enough to evade the GitHub search and API paths normally used to find this kind of compromise,” they wrote. How the attacks worked The attackers planted execution hooks for AI coding assistants and development tools, including Claude, Gemini, Cursor, and VS Code, alongside polymorphic wrappers measuring 12.9 to 13.7 MB that decode a hidden CI-publisher payload. Separately, the npm worm steals credentials, modifies repositories and CI configurations, and spreads through npm packages. The malware also uses a compiled native add-on to decrypt and launch a separate payload. Before executing, the loader checks for CI runners, containers, sandboxes, debuggers, and other signs of automated analysis, exiting silently when it detects them to reduce the likelihood of detection by security scanners. The researchers also found a second build that skips the encrypted file. “It forks, detaches and runs a hard-coded command that pulls a loader from a repository on the operator's own GitHub account,” they wrote. That account – CementBeetleSteeple – hosted 17 campaign repositories in total. JFrog connected this account to a shellpanel scanner, previously documented by Socket in a large-scale campaign that abused GitHub Actions in compromised repositories to exploit CVE-2026-41940 and steal server credentials. item.title: Alibaba's Qwen AI caught trying to contact server in China
item.description: Open-weight models from China have become very popular, but they've also raised some security suspicions. Cohere, a Canada-based biz that offers AI models to enterprises, says that when it was testing Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next in its evaluation sandbox, the model attempted to send data to China. "Asked to write a defensive detection rule, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next ignored instructions and inventoried the machine it was running on and then tried to upload a probe file to an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket in Beijing," the biz said in a blog post on Monday. Cohere was running the model through CTI-REALM, Microsoft's security analyst benchmark, and gave Qwen the task of writing a detection rule to look for malicious file downloading and execution by watching for invocations of curl processing bash scripts to the /tmp directory that were accompanied by bash execution. The model's "reasoning" output invented a prior conversation and asserted that no tools were used, output that a guardrail system reading chain-of-thought would accept. Nonetheless, the model issued a curl command to an Alibaba Cloud (aliyuncs.com) server. "The model listed everything in /tmp, checked which transfer tools were installed, read the machine's DNS settings, then tried to upload a test string to an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket in Beijing and checked whether it worked," Cohere said. "Our sandbox had no route out, so the request died at the container wall." The Cohere team wonders aloud whether that behavior was intended, but has no answer. "The first issue is that it made a network call at all," Ivan Zhang, co-founder of Cohere, told The Register via email. "The model was asked to write a detection rule, which doesn't require external communication, and its reasoning trace said it wouldn't use tools. The destination raises additional questions because the attempted upload was to an Alibaba Cloud storage endpoint that wasn't part of the task. We don't know why it appeared, and we don't know the root cause." Alibaba, the maker of the model, did not respond to a request to address Cohere's concerns. Asked whether Cohere ran similar tests against US-made open-weight models, Zhang said, "We evaluate a broad range of models using the same framework our customers use in production: agents with access to real tools operating inside controlled environments. "The key point isn't a comparison between providers. What made this noteworthy was that the model took actions unrelated to the task and those actions weren't reflected in its reasoning trace. The behavior appeared in fewer than one in 100,000 calls, which is exactly why large-scale testing and monitoring matter." There have been other unsubstantiated claims made about similar behavior from open-weight models, and such reports have suggested that "hallucination" - errors made by these models - may be the cause. item.title: LiteLLM supply chain attack started with an exposed master key
item.description: LiteLLM has traced last week’s supply chain attack to a master key it accidentally committed to a public GitHub repository in May. The cloud and AI model secret-stealing part of the incident began when someone uploaded a poisoned version (1.107.0) of the popular open source AI gateway to PyPI and its container registries last Wednesday. This compromised version contained an infostealer and a remote access trojan capable of executing arbitrary code on infected machines. While the trojanized package was available on PyPI for less than two hours before being quarantined, it received about 49,000 downloads during that time, according to Wiz. On Friday, LiteLLM detailed the attack chain behind the compromised release and traced it back to May 27, when a configuration file containing a master key was committed to the public LiteLLM-Labs/lite-harness repository. The key belonged to an open source tool used internally by LiteLLM to orchestrate AI agents. The project's developers quickly spotted the error and removed the exposed commit, but failed to revoke the master key. “On October 10th, the threat actor used this key to gain access to our LiteLLM Agent Platform and extracted this GitHub CLI OAuth token,” according to Friday’s postmortem . “From this point onwards, the threat actor had owner-level access to all repositories in our GitHub.” This is especially serious because GitHub CLI tokens are “post-2fa,” meaning that they don’t trigger GitHub's sudo mode authentication flows typically required to perform high-impact repository actions. The token allowed the attacker to author malicious commits into branches on other internal repos - including workflows designed to steal any tokens and secrets configured to be available during the continuous integration development process. And this allowed them to steal other GitHub CLI OAuth tokens linked to two engineers with maintainer privileges. Plus, they acquired tokens for several other internal systems, we’re told. “Reviewing the actor's activity on these other systems shows attempts to identify and exfiltrate additional keys and tokens, with a primary focus on upstream inference API tokens,” LiteLLM noted. Having now stolen several privileged identities, the miscreant could make changes to GitHub repositories without raising any suspicion because the actions and approvals all appeared to come from legitimate, credentialed engineers. In response, LiteLLM’s developers are revoking every token associated with every internal system and vendor platform. “This incident has provided a strong illustration of the risks associated with failing to rotate a potentially exposed key,” they wrote. item.title: Microsoft offers parachutes to 60k employees if they jump by the end of the year
item.description: Microsoft, on Monday, announced a voluntary exit offer open to about one quarter of its employees. The company’s HR chief, Amy Coleman, explained the deal in a letter later posted to Redmond's corporate blog. While scant on specifics, Coleman’s note dangles an opportunity for anyone considering a move to get out while the getting’s good. Eligible employees in participating organizations “who may be considering a future outside the company,” Coleman wrote, can seize “the opportunity to leave Microsoft with financial support and career planning resources." Microsoft tells us that 60,000 of its employees in the UK, US, Canada, and India are being given the opportunity to take the VEO. Microsoft told us it isn't classifying the deal as a buyout since no one is being incentivized to leave. We’re told that the offer is akin to a standard severance deal in terms of monetary and career assistance bonuses. Some employees will also be given the option for extended healthcare and stock shares. The company declined to get specific on which roles or teams are up for the exit offer, but Coleman’s note does state that employees in those four markets up to employment level 70 will be eligible, which translates to everyone at or below the VP level. “Some organizations are providing the Voluntary Exit Offer, and some are not,” Coleman’s note stated. “Participation varies based on each business’s priorities, customer commitments and workforce needs.” Microsoft employed around 223,000 people as of June, 2026 when it issued its last annual report, and since then has eliminated around 4,800 roles . By that count, the VEO is being offered to around a quarter of Microsoft’s remaining employees, though Microsoft tells us it doesn’t expect everyone to take the offer. Microsoft said it doesn't have a target number for the VEO. Google, which made a similar offer to employees in 2025, saw between three and five percent of those eligible take the offer. If that holds in Microsoft's case, anywhere between 1,800 and 3,000 employees could accept the deal before the window closes on December 31. It would be easy to blame increasing automation for the plans to reduce staff, but Microsoft insisted otherwise in our conversation. The verbiage about "changing needs" isn’t a euphemism for AI, in other words. Rather, we're told, the deal reflects the success of a previous early retirement offer from April, which saw Microsoft extend a voluntary buyout to employees whose age plus years of employment at Microsoft exceeded 70. The April offer only applied to around 9,000 employees, and Microsoft said it received feedback from others who would've taken it if it had been available to them. What could Redmond do but acquiesce? Especially given those recent earnings that saw Microsoft make serious bank across its portfolio. As we well know from watching the tech industry over the years, big earnings is the perfect time to shave off some headcount to keep the line going up. ®

item.description: To address a vulnerability in Google's Brotli compression technology that could allow attackers to corrupt process memory, Microsoft is urging .NET users to update "as soon as possible" after releasing an out-of-band (OOB) security update. It released new versions for .NET 8, 9, 10, and .NET 11 to patch against the Brotli bug, following similar updates from Node.js, Python, and other projects. Senior program manager Rahul Bhandari said in the October 25 release that the buffer overflow vulnerability in Brotli, tracked as CVE-2026-111497 and rated 8.1 under CVSS v3.1 in Microsoft's advisory, could allow an unauthenticated attacker to read or corrupt process memory, potentially resulting in information disclosure, denial of service, or elevation of privilege. Microsoft’s own advisory for the vulnerability, which some are referring to as Broccoli2Shell or Node2Shell, confirms that while experts have cobbled working exploits together , there is nothing to suggest that criminals are using them in successful attacks. However, its exploitability assessment reads: “Exploitation More Likely.” Broccoli2Shell was first disclosed on October 21 by the Node.js team, which released fixes for ten vulnerabilities, the most serious of which was CVE-2026-111497. Node.js credited Khai Tran and Sylvie Mayer of OpenAI’s Codex Security with the discovery, but failed to mention why it was only recognized as a security flaw and disclosed properly in October, despite the underlying bug having been fixed in Brotli's source code in February. OpenAI filled in the gap with a Xeet : “This root cause issue was actually fixed in the Brotli source code in February, but it wasn’t known at the time that it gave rise to a security vulnerability, and there was no more recent release of Brotli. “Since Brotli is built into other software, any software which includes this library needs to take the update too, followed by the users of that software.” Attackers can exploit vulnerable systems by providing them with malicious Brotli-compressed data via a specially crafted request. The vulnerability went slightly under the radar due to the disclosure timing closely aligning with that of PHP2Shell , although fixing the critical flaw should be a priority due to the range of technologies that are affected. item.title: Open source keyboard lets you swap parts like magnetic Lego bricks
item.description: The world is full of different keyboard layouts, but if you want one that's completely customized, down to the individual key, there's a new open source project that uses magnets to hold interchangeable pieces together. Keybytes is an open source project that allows any ambitious builder to create a fully modular keyboard - and we’re talking FULLY modular here. Each key contains its own RISC-V microcontroller and pogo pins on all four sides, providing power and I2C connections between adjacent modules so users can rearrange the keys into different layouts. The only extra component needed is a controller module, which coordinates the individual keys and handles communication with the host computer. And good news: Despite consisting of two stacked circuit boards, it has the same footprint as the single-key modules that attach to it. The entire thing was designed by a Massachusetts Institute of Technology freshman named Nathan Alspaugh, who is studying aerospace engineering. Alspaugh has always wanted to design his own keyboard, and who better than an MIT student to go over the top in building the most intricate, overengineered version imaginable? “I had always wanted to make a keyboard but I didn't want to be locked into just one design so I wanna make it so that I can rearrange it at any time,” Alspaugh said in the first entry of his project journal , which he’s been keeping since March of this year. “I searched online and couldn't find it anywhere so I decided to make it myself.” The main readme in the GitHub project isn’t super detailed, instead mostly describing what the project entails for anyone willing to give it a shot (custom printed circuit boards, Cherry MX switches, 3D-printed cases, and a whole lot of tiny soldered components). It’s Alspaugh’s journal where the depth of the work he did is laid bare for all to see, and boy did he do a lot of work. Designing a single-key modular keyboard from scratch is no easy task, and the journal details a number of setbacks that Alspaugh faced, like magnets that wouldn’t stay put, design compromises, and - of course - plenty of board errors that he luckily was able to catch in the design phase before spending a bunch of cash ordering custom components. Alspaugh also had to learn to use a resin 3D printer for the project, and of course multiple iterations and a bunch of manual modifications had to be made to get everything to properly fit together. Alspaugh told The Register he’s spent around 100 hours on the project so far. And then there’s the cost: All those tiny custom boards don’t come cheap. According to a shopping cart for the board designs included in his journal, the Keybits (the individual key control boards) cost only a couple of bucks apiece, but the Keywords (controller boards) cost $30 a pop. item.title: Reddit's r/opensource bans AI slop, and quite a few humans for good measure
item.description: Reddit's r/opensource community has declared war on AI-generated software by introducing a sweeping set of new rules that also manage to shut out solo developers, newcomers, and anyone who doesn't speak English. The crackdown , announced over the weekend, bans projects that use AI, that were created with AI, or that are intended for AI applications. "The long story short, if your project uses AI, is made by AI, or is intended for AI, it's not welcome on r/opensource," moderator Wolvereness wrote. "AI, as it exists today, is incongruent to this Open Source community." To get a project featured on the subreddit, developers now need to show it has been actively maintained for at least a year, has an established community, and has at least three contributors, give or take. Student projects such as note-taking apps and PDF viewers aren't welcome either, and developers can no longer use the subreddit to find people willing to help maintain their software. That creates a chicken-and-egg problem for independent developers, who apparently need an established community before they can use an open source forum to find one. Even projects with no AI involvement could fall foul of the rules. One Reddit user pointed out that their nine-year-old project, which has more than 300 GitHub stars and dozens of resolved issues, would no longer qualify because they're its sole contributor. The moderator also imposed a minimum Reddit account age of one year and requires significant prior contributions. Anyone who attempts to post and then contacts the moderators seeking an exception risks being permanently banned and muted. Perhaps the most eyebrow-raising restriction concerns language. "If you don't speak English, you need to find a different community," the announcement states. Moderators say they cannot distinguish AI-written content from AI-translated text, and that non-English speakers cannot verify whether a translation is accurate. That particular rule has gone down about as well as you might expect. Fellow moderator ssddanbrown publicly objected, saying they hadn't been consulted about the changes and only learned of them through moderation notifications. "I don't agree with that rule. Especially so with how it was said," they wrote. The rules also raise awkward questions about projects like Linux, whose developers have taken a different approach to AI-assisted contributions. The kernel allows developers to use the technology while holding them responsible for the resulting code. Earlier this month, maintainers even decided to drop the requirement to disclose AI assistance . Asked whether that meant Linux would be banned from r/opensource, Wolvereness suggested it would probably still be allowed, arguing that enforcement would depend on whether a project was obviously the product of AI-generated code. item.title: UK pentester 'killa' claims $2K Bitcoin prize in PHP2Shell capture-the-flag contest
item.description: A UK-based developer and pentester has claimed a $2,000 Bitcoin prize for demonstrating the exploitability of the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities that melted the internet last week. Jaydip Modhwadia, 26, otherwise known as “Killa,” claimed the prize set by James Pavur, who launched the "Steal My Bitcoin" site on October 24. Pavur launched the CTF (capture the flag) challenge to prove that the PHP2Shell exploit was not as easy as those in the cybersecurity community claimed it to be, promising to award $2,000 in Bitcoin to anyone who could achieve Remote Code Execution (RCE) on his website. "My Bitcoin was stolen after 19.28 hours," the website now says, after Modhwadia claimed the prize, although the real time taken is thought to be less than three hours. Soon after Pavur launched the CTF on Saturday, prospective flag-catchers complained that the website he set up, which served only static HTML, was not built in a way that allowed the PHP2Shell exploit to achieve RCE. The web page was running a vulnerable version of PHP, but the exploit path required a vulnerable website to serve a PHP file for flag-catchers to use as a hook – something that Pavur seemingly updated at around 1300 UTC on October 25. Modhwadia achieved RCE on the website, exposing a PHP endpoint, at 1547 UTC. After an error from Pavur placing the wrong wallet key on the server, the CTF creator sent Modhwadia his award, which the community upped to $2,000 from Pavur’s initial $500. The pentester published a write-up of his method, a single-file Python script he says requires 20 HTTP requests "at most" to fully execute. Speaking to The Register , Modhwadia also confirmed that he got the flag in "around three or so hours in total." He said he followed the news about the competition, "but didn't attempt it until it gained significant notice." If he had attempted it before Pavur introduced the endpoint, he may have struggled. For hours, bug bounty hunters were trying to access the website to attempt the challenge, as news of the CTF had exploded across tech circles. "The fact that it took 19 hours was because after it went popular, the entire site became basically unusable for anyone at all," Modhwadia added. The challenge saw a huge number of attempts, despite Pavur's decision to introduce a prohibitive 1MB request limit on Nginx. Alon Gal, co-founder and CTO at Hudson Rock, commended Modhwadia's work, but added that his success achieved in just a few hours should not be taken to mean that the same attack could be automated at scale. He said : "Does this mean autonomous AI agents can now compromise arbitrary PHP servers at scale? No. This was a sophisticated, target-specific exploit. "But it does demonstrate that PHP2Shell can be weaponized against a live target, even with meaningful technical constraints." item.title: Trumpets blare and skies part as AI hypefest culminates in Anthropic IPO filing
item.description: Anthropic has filed for an IPO that could rank among Wall Street's biggest ever, revealing an $80.7 billion half-year loss, a startlingly complex governance structure, and warnings that its AI models could blackmail humans, resist shutdown, or create "existential risks" to society. The Claude maker filed its S-1 registration statement with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday as it prepares to list on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. The company has not yet disclosed its proposed share price or how many shares it plans to sell. Of the filing's 614 pages, 94 are devoted to risk factors. But it's Anthropic's financial figures that are likely to raise eyebrows first. The Claude maker reported $16.3 billion in revenue for the first six months of 2026, up from $1.2 billion a year earlier. It also posted a whopping $80.7 billion net loss, although $72.4 billion of that was an accounting adjustment tied to the company's soaring valuation, not money it actually spent. Anthropic's operating loss was considerably smaller at $693 million, down from $2.1 billion a year earlier. By its own adjusted accounting, the company made a $1.6 billion operating profit in the first half of 2026, for a margin of around 10 percent. Whether it can keep making money on those terms is another matter. Training and running Claude requires an eye-watering amount of computing power, and Anthropic will need much more to keep pace with its rivals. A $1.6 billion adjusted profit won't count for much if the infrastructure bills keep growing faster than the business. Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, told The Register that Anthropic's IPO could leave ordinary investors paying a premium for growth that has yet to translate into sustained profits. "A huge pool of private capital has allowed AI businesses to scale up and command extraordinary valuations long before they reach the stock market," she said, adding that investors buying in at the IPO will face a price with "a hefty dose of future success baked in." The financial risks are fairly conventional by Silicon Valley standards, but the warnings about what Claude might get up to are perhaps less so. Anthropic claims that models, including its own, have exhibited unexpected or self-preserving behavior, including attempts to resist shutdown, conceal information, and produce outputs resembling blackmail. It also warns that sufficiently advanced AI systems could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to society” if deployed without adequate safeguards. That's not to say Claude is currently blackmailing customers. Anthropic has observed some of this behavior in testing, but it also identifies more immediate security concerns as it gives its models access to external tools, code repositories, and corporate systems.
